title: AI tools: context and memory
summary: What an AI coding tool really sees, why long chats go wrong, and what to write in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md.

text: An AI model doesn't remember you. Each time it answers, it reads one block of text: its context window.
- Everything in that block counts: instructions, your messages, its answers, the files it read, the outputs of the commands it ran.
- Anything outside it doesn't exist for the model: yesterday's chat, a file it didn't open.
A new session starts empty, except for what the tool loads at the start.
The window has a size, counted in tokens: pieces of text, often a short word or part of a longer one.
- Every message, file and output uses tokens. One big log can fill a good part of it at once.
- When it gets close to full, the tool summarizes or drops the oldest parts, and details get lost: an exact rule, a decision. A very long chat slowly gets worse.

scheme: hour 1   goal, a rule, first try     ✘
the AI tries the first fix again
text: In a long chat, failed attempts stay in view and pull the model back, while the first rules fade into a summary.
- One task per session: when you change task, start fresh.
- Stuck after several tries? Start again with a short summary: the goal, what failed, what you decided.
- Claude Code calls it /clear (start empty) and /compact (keep a summary). Other tools have a "new chat" button.

scheme: ├── AGENTS.md     read by many AI tools
text: To give the AI the same knowledge every time, write it in a file the tool loads at the start of each session, like notes for a new teammate.
- AGENTS.md is shared by many tools (Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Zed…). Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, or AGENTS.md when there is no CLAUDE.md.
- Some tools also write notes of their own: a memory. Read them now and then: a wrong note comes back in every session.

scheme: ✘ the whole history of the project
text: Keep the file short and specific: it's loaded every time, each line costs room, and a long file buries the rules that matter.
- Yes: how to build and test, conventions, what not to touch, the why of an unusual choice.
- No secrets: the file is usually committed, and all of it is sent to the model.
- No copy of the code: the AI opens the code when it needs it. Claude Code's docs advise under 200 lines.

scheme: │  checked by the tool, every time
text: An instruction file is advice, not a lock. The model reads it and usually follows it, but nothing forces it to.
- A rule that must always hold (never deploy, never delete data) goes where the tool enforces it: permission settings, or a hook that refuses the command.
- Safest of all: don't give the AI the keys it must never use.
